nodes.name: Molybdenum Carbide Synthesis
nodes.procedure: A series of samples of MoC were synthesized. The detailed steps for materials synthesis can be found in the Supporting Information and in Figure S1.

nodes.source_text: The double-layer capacitance (Cdl) values of Ru@NMoC were 26.8 mF cm^-2 in 1 M KOH, 21.65 mF cm^-2 in 1 M KOH + 0.5 M NaCl, and 17.36 mF cm^-2 in 1 M KOH seawater. These values are notably higher than those of Ru@MoC, 20% Pt/C and Ru/C, confirming the superior proton and electron transport capabilities of Ru@NMoC.

The specific surface areas of Ru@NMoC and Ru@MoC were measured using the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller specific surface area method. The specific surface areas of the two are roughly equal, indicating that the introduction of N has no effect on the size of the specific surface area.

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD shows MoC, NMoC, and Ru@NMoC samples exhibit distinct diffraction peaks at 36.7°, 42.3°, 61.6°, and 74.0° corresponding to (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes of pure MoC phase (JCPDS No. 89-2868). Nitrogen doping and ruthenium clusters do not alter the phase structure of MoC substrate. Absence of Ru diffraction peaks indicates Ru exists as ultrafine nanoclusters within MoC substrate.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The physical phases of Ru@NMoC catalysts were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD). As shown in Figure 1b, MoC, NMoC, and Ru@NMoC samples exhibited distinct diffraction peaks at approximately 36.7°, 42.3°, 61.6°, and 74.0°, corresponding to the (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes of the pure MoC phase (JCPDS No. 89-2868), respectively. Notably, the introduction of nitrogen doping to MoC and ruthenium clusters did not alter the phase structure of MoC substrate matrix. Furthermore, the absence of diffraction peaks associated with Ru in the XRD pattern of Ru@NMoC supports the hypothesis that Ru exists as ultrafine nanoclusters covered within MoC substrate.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM images reveal synthesized catalyst exhibits spherical nanoflower structure with size of approximately 350 nm. Morphology of NMoC matrix remains unchanged after incorporation of Ru clusters.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The morphologies of 3 wt% Ru@NMoC, 3.5 wt% Ru@NMoC, and 4 wt% Ru@NMoC with different Ru contents were examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figure S2a-c). SEM images reveal that the synthesized catalyst exhibits a spherical nanoflower structure with a size of approximately 350 nm. Importantly, the morphology of the NMoC matrix remains unchanged after the incorporation of Ru clusters (Figure S3a-c).

nodes.characterization_summary: Raman spectroscopy shows all three samples display two distinct vibrational peaks at approximately 1350 and 1600 cm⁻¹, corresponding to D and G bands of amorphous carbon. High ID/IG ratio indicates large number of defects that enhance electronic transport properties.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Ru@NMoC catalysts were further characterized using Raman spectroscopy. As shown in Figure 2a, all three samples displayed two distinct vibrational peaks at approximately 1350 and 1600 cm⁻¹, corresponding to bands D and G of amorphous carbon, respectively. These peaks are associated with carbon defects and sp²-hybridized graphitic carbon. Three of the materials have a high ID/IG ratio, indicating that the three synthetic materials have a large number of defects.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru 3p XPS spectrum reveals Ru@NMoC catalyst exhibits slightly positive shift compared to Ru and Ru@MoC, indicating reoptimization of charge transfer of Ru cluster on MoC by N doping makes Ru cluster have fewer electrons than in Ru@MoC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Figure 2b, Ru 3p X-ray photoelectronic spectroscopy (XPS) spectrum reveals that Ru@NMoC catalyst exhibits a slightly positive shift compared to Ru and Ru@MoC. This indicates that the reoptimization of the charge transfer of the Ru cluster on MoC by doping with N heteroatoms makes the Ru cluster in Ru@NMoC have fewer electrons around it than the Ru cluster in Ru@MoC, which is consistent with the results of subsequent theoretical calculations.

nodes.characterization_summary: Mo 3d XPS spectra display three sets of peaks corresponding to Mo²⁺ (228.8 and 231.3 eV), Mo⁴⁺ (228.9 and 232.9 eV), and Mo⁶⁺ (231.8 and 235.5 eV). Introduction of nitrogen into MoC substrate caused positive shift in Mo 3d spectrum, indicative of electron transfer from Mo to N. Continued positive shift upon addition of Ru clusters suggests additional electron transfer from Mo to Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Mo 3d XPS spectra (Figure 2c) displays three sets of peaks correspond respectively to Mo²⁺ (228.8 and 231.3 eV), Mo⁴⁺ (228.9 and 232.9 eV), and Mo⁶⁺ (231.8 and 235.5 eV) scattering. The introduction of nitrogen into MoC substrate caused a positive shift in Mo 3d spectrum, indicative of electron transfer from Mo to N. Furthermore, the continued positive shift in the spectrum upon the addition of Ru clusters suggests additional electron transfer from Mo to Ru, in agreement with subsequent theoretical calculations.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ XPS spectra monitor changes in valence state of Ru@NMoC catalyst during HER process. At cathodic potential of -0.04 V, slight shift in Ru 3p spectrum toward lower binding energy observed, indicating Ru entered more electron-rich state. Mo 3d binding energies showed no appreciable shift. N 1s spectrum remained largely unchanged, signifying robustness of Mo-N-C active sites. Over 100-h test, Ru 3p spectrum remained stable. Mo⁶⁺ peak intensity gradually decreased, indicating progressive reduction of Mo oxides. N 1s spectrum remained essentially unchanged.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In situ XPS spectra of Ru@NMoC catalyst was employed to monitor changes in the valence state of Ru@NMoC catalyst during HER process (Figure 4a-c). As shown in Figure 4a, when the cathodic potential was increased to -0.04 V, a slight shift in the Ru 3p spectrum toward lower binding energy was observed. This indicates that Ru entered a more electron-rich state during the reaction, which likely enhances catalytic activity. At higher potentials, the Ru 3p binding energies showed no further appreciable shift, suggesting that Ru@NMoC catalyst achieved a stable electronic state under these conditions. Similarly, no appreciable shift was detected in the Mo 3d binding energies upon increasing the cathodic potential (Figure 4b). N 1 s spectrum, as illustrated in Figure 4c, remained largely unchanged throughout the reaction, signifying the robustness of Mo-N-C active sites. Over the course of the 100-h test, Ru 3p spectrum remained stable, as depicted in Figure 4d, indicating that the catalyst's structure and electronic properties were largely preserved throughout the reaction. However, as shown in Figure 4e, the intensity of Mo⁶⁺ peak in Mo 3d spectrum gradually decreased over the reaction time, indicating the progressive reduction of Mo oxides in the catalyst. As shown in Figure 4f, the N 1 s spectrum remained essentially unchanged throughout the long reaction time, indicating the stability of the active site.

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman spectroscopy at varying potentials shows broad Raman peak near 3500 cm⁻¹ attributed to interfacial water. Upon deconvolution, separated into three components at 3225 cm⁻¹ (v₁), 3450 cm⁻¹ (v₂), and 3615 cm⁻¹ (v₃). v₁ and v₂ vibrations correspond to tetrahedral and trihedral coordination water molecules actively participating in HER. v₃ vibration associated with dangling O-H bonds, inactive for HER. As HER potential increases, v₃ peak occupancy decreases more for Ru@NMoC compared to Ru@MoC, indicating Ru@NMoC more capable of cleaving water bonds.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To further evaluate the water dissociation capability of Ru@NMoC, in situ Raman spectroscopy was conducted at varying potentials. As shown in Figure 4g-h, a broad Raman peak near 3500 cm⁻¹ was observed, attributed to interfacial water at the catalyst-electrolyte interface. Upon deconvolution, this peak was separated into three components at 3225 cm⁻¹ (v₁), 3450 cm⁻¹ (v₂), and 3615 cm⁻¹ (v₃). The v₁ and v₂ vibrations correspond to tetrahedral and trihedral coordination water molecules, respectively, both of which actively participate in HER. In contrast, the v₃ vibration is associated with dangling O-H bonds in interfacial water, which are inactive for HER. Notably, as the HER potential increases, the v₃ peak occupancy decreases more for Ru@NMoC compared to Ru@MoC. This suggests that as the presence of inactive water species decreases with increasing potential, Ru@NMoC is more capable of cleaving water bonds, thereby improving the proton supply and catalytic efficiency of the HER process.
